claim: Around 90% of solid tumors have aneuploid karyotypes
source: However, around 90% of solid tumors have aneuploid karyotypes (Ben-David et al., 2019; Taylor et al., 2018), raising the question of how cancer cells can tolerate the massive amount of transcriptomic and proteomic changes.
evidence: Supported by citations to Ben-David et al., 2019 and Taylor et al., 2018

claim: Previous studies demonstrated correlated expression between gene copy number and transcriptome level for genes on aneuploid chromosomes
source: Previous studies demonstrated correlated expression between gene copy number and transcriptome level for genes on aneuploid chromosomes while there is a buffering effect at the proteome level adjusting protein levels, especially for protein complex subunits (Stingele et al., 2012; Dephoure et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Stingele et al., 2012 and Dephoure et al., 2014

claim: There is a buffering effect at the proteome level adjusting protein levels, especially for protein complex subunits
source: Previous studies demonstrated correlated expression between gene copy number and transcriptome level for genes on aneuploid chromosomes while there is a buffering effect at the proteome level adjusting protein levels, especially for protein complex subunits (Stingele et al., 2012; Dephoure et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Stingele et al., 2012 and Dephoure et al., 2014

claim: Post-transcriptional compensatory mechanism preventing excess translation of complex members has been characterized for copy number alterations in yeast
source: This post-transcriptional compensatory mechanism preventing excess translation of complex members has also been characterized for copy number alterations (CNAs) in different contexts such as yeast (Ishikawa et al., 2017) and cancer (Gonçalves et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ishikawa et al., 2017

claim: Post-transcriptional compensatory mechanism preventing excess translation of complex members has been characterized for copy number alterations in cancer
source: This post-transcriptional compensatory mechanism preventing excess translation of complex members has also been characterized for copy number alterations (CNAs) in different contexts such as yeast (Ishikawa et al., 2017) and cancer (Gonçalves et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gonçalves et al., 2017

claim: Proteins with larger interface size showed larger degree of buffering
source: Structural properties of proteins have an effect on the degree of post-transcriptional buffering on changes induced by CNAs, for example, proteins with larger interface size showed larger degree of buffering (Sousa et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sousa et al., 2019

claim: Post-translational regulation has been identified as a dosage compensation mechanism in response to aneuploidy in cancer cell lines
source: Recently, post-translational regulation has also been identified as a dosage compensation mechanism in response to aneuploidy in cancer cell lines (Schukken and Sheltzer, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schukken and Sheltzer, 2021

claim: Aneuploidy largely affects expression of genes on other chromosomes
source: Transcriptome analysis revealed that aneuploidy largely affects expression of genes on other chromosomes too (Nawata et al., 2011; Upender et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Nawata et al., 2011 and Upender et al., 2004

claim: A correlated increase in the abundance of co-complex members encoded by genes outside the copy number amplified region has been shown for CNAs
source: For CNAs, a correlated increase in the abundance of co-complex members encoded by genes outside the copy number amplified region has been shown (Gonçalves et al., 2017) raising the question of whether this could contribute to the expression changes in aneuploid cells even on diploid chromosomes.
evidence: Supported by citation to Gonçalves et al., 2017

claim: 203 whole-chromosome-level alterations including 86 amplifications and 117 deletions were detected for 32 cancer types
source: In total, we detected 203 whole-chromosome-level alterations including 86 amplifications and 117 deletions for 32 cancer types (Figure 1B, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Based on analysis of TCGA data as described in the manuscript

claim: On average 41% and 48% of the genes located on amplified and deleted chromosomes, respectively, changed expression
source: We found that on average 41% and 48% of the genes located on amplified and deleted chromosomes, respectively, changed expression (Figure 1C).
evidence: Based on differential expression analysis of TCGA data and shown in Figure 1C

claim: 15 and 18% of genes on average for amplification and deletion cases, respectively, show expression changes on other, typically diploid chromosomes
source: Besides those intuitively expected gene expression changes on the aneuploid chromosomes, we observed a surprisingly large number of expression changes happening on other, typically diploid chromosomes (15 and 18% of genes on average for amplification and deletion cases, respectively; Figure 1C).
evidence: Based on differential expression analysis of TCGA data and shown in Figure 1C

claim: 305 co-amplifications occurred more frequently than expected by chance covering 60 out of 86 cancer-type-specific amplifications
source: For the 86 cancer-type-specific amplifications, we identified 305 co-amplifications that occurred more frequently than expected by chance covering 60 out of 86 cancer-type-specific amplifications (adjusted p-value <0.01, chi-square test; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Based on chi-square test analysis of TCGA data

claim: There is no significant difference between the medians of co-amplified and non-co-amplified chromosomes in terms of contribution to transcriptional dysregulation
source: We found that there is no significant difference between the medians of these chromosome groups (p=0.4, paired Wilcoxon test; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, C) suggesting that they do not substantially contribute to the overall transcriptional dysregulation on other chromosomes.
evidence: Based on paired Wilcoxon test analysis and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, C

claim: A smaller number of proteins showed abundance changes compared to observations at the transcriptome level
source: We observed that a smaller number of proteins showed abundance changes compared to our observations at the transcriptome level (after normalizing for the largely different gene coverage between the transcriptomics and proteomics datasets) both for amplification and deletion cases (Figure 1C).
evidence: Based on comparison of transcriptomic and proteomic data from TCGA/CPTAC and shown in Figure 1C

claim: GO terms belonging to cell cycle and cell cycle processes are among the top dysregulated gene sets
source: Indeed, we found gene ontology (GO) terms belonging to cell cycle and cell cycle processes to be among the top dysregulated gene sets (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Based on GO enrichment analysis of dysregulated genes

claim: Differentially abundant proteins of other chromosomes tend to be complex partners of differentially abundant proteins from the aneuploid chromosome for both whole-chromosome-level amplifications and deletions
source: We observed a general tendency for the differentially abundant proteins of other chromosomes to be complex partners of differentially abundant proteins from the aneuploid chromosome for both whole-chromosome-level amplifications and deletions (p<0.05, chi-square test; Figure 2A).
evidence: Based on chi-square test analysis using CORUM complex data and shown in Figure 2A

claim: On average 4.47% of differentially abundant proteins on other chromosomes are partners of those on aneuploid proteins
source: We found a moderate percentage (in average 4.47%; Supplementary file 3) of differentially abundant proteins on other chromosomes being partners of those on aneuploid proteins.
evidence: Based on analysis of CORUM complex data

claim: When only proteins participating in at least one complex were considered, the average fraction of partner proteins among differentially abundant proteins increased to 12.61%
source: However, the coverage of proteins with CORUM complex information is rather limited (22% of proteins form part of at least one complex in CORUM). When only proteins participating in at least one complex were considered, the average fraction of partner proteins among differentially abundant proteins increased to 12.61% (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Based on analysis of CORUM complex data

claim: Protein abundance correlations between differentially abundant proteins on aneuploid chromosomes and their co-complex members are significantly stronger than with non-complex members
source: Moreover, comparing protein abundance correlations between differentially abundant proteins on aneuploid chromosomes and their co-complex members with non-complex members showed significantly stronger correlations between proteins of same complexes (p<2.2e-16, Wilcoxon test; Figure 2B).
evidence: Based on Wilcoxon test analysis of protein abundance correlations and shown in Figure 2B

claim: An enrichment of interactions between differentially abundant proteins encoded on the aneuploid and those on other chromosomes was found in 9 out of 13 cancer-type-specific amplifications and 8 of the 20 deletions
source: Indeed, we found an enrichment of interactions between those protein sets in 9 out of 13 cancer-type-specific amplifications and 8 of the 20 deletions (p<0.05, randomization test; Figure 2C, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: Based on randomization test using HIPPIE PPI data and shown in Figure 2C

claim: On average 27.5% of the differentially abundant proteins on other chromosomes interact with those on the aneuploid chromosomes
source: We found that on average 27.5% of the differentially abundant proteins on other chromosomes interact with those on the aneuploid chromosomes (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: Based on analysis of HIPPIE PPI data

claim: Complex subunits are significantly depleted in differentially abundant proteins on other chromosomes for amplification cases
source: As a result of this, we found a significant depletion of complex subunits in differentially abundant proteins on other chromosomes for amplification cases (p<0.05, chi-square test; Figure 2D).
evidence: Based on chi-square test analysis using CORUM complex data and shown in Figure 2D

claim: Differentially abundant proteins of other chromosomes are significantly enriched in complex proteins in the case of chromosomal deletions
source: This effect was not observed in the case of chromosomal deletions in which differentially abundant proteins of other chromosomes are significantly enriched in complex proteins (p<0.05, chi-square test; Figure 2D).
evidence: Based on chi-square test analysis using CORUM complex data and shown in Figure 2D

claim: Downregulated genes are significantly related to higher methylation levels in aneuploid samples in only 6 amplification cases out of 86 (~7%) and in 5 deletion cases out of 117 (~4%)
source: We found that downregulated genes are significantly related to higher methylation levels in aneuploid samples in only 6 amplification cases out of 86 (~7%) and in 5 deletion cases out of 117 (~4%; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Based on DNA methylation analysis and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A

claim: Significant associations between lower methylation level and upregulated genes in aneuploid samples were observed for 10 out of 86 amplification cases and 16 out of 117 deletion cases
source: We observed significant associations between lower methylation level and upregulated genes in aneuploid samples for few cases (10 out of 86 amplification cases and 16 out of 117 deletion cases) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Based on DNA methylation analysis and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B

claim: Epigenetic regulation does not have a substantial contribution to genome-wide changes in gene expression induced by aneuploidy
source: This suggests that epigenetic regulation does not have a substantial contribution to the described genome-wide changes in gene expression induced by aneuploidy.
evidence: Inferred from the low number of cases showing significant methylation associations

claim: Performing a randomization test did not reveal an excess of targets of differentially expressed TFs on the aneuploid chromosome among differentially expressed genes on other chromosomes for any of the tested cancer-type-specific chromosomes
source: Performing a randomization test did not reveal an excess of targets for any of the tested, cancer-type-specific chromosomes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Based on randomization test using ENCODE TF-target data and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C

claim: Top correlated co-complex members of aneuploid proteins have significantly higher numbers of ubiquitination sites
source: Indeed we found that top correlated partners have significantly higher numbers of ubiquitination sites (p<0.05, Wilcoxon test; Figure 3B).
evidence: Based on Wilcoxon test analysis using PhosphoSitePlus ubiquitination data and shown in Figure 3B

claim: A primary mechanism for keeping protein complex stoichiometry in check is post-translational regulation such as ubiquitin-mediated degradation
source: This suggests that a primary mechanism for keeping protein complex stoichiometry in check seems to be indeed post-translational regulation (such as ubiquitin-mediated degradation).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that top correlated partners have higher ubiquitination sites

claim: Aggregation-prone proteins on amplified chromosomes show stronger correlations with their complex partners on other chromosomes compared to non-aggregating counterparts
source: Indeed, we observed stronger correlations for aggregation-prone proteins as compared to their non-aggregating counterparts (p<2.2e-16, Wilcoxon test; Figure 4A).
evidence: Based on Wilcoxon test analysis using aggregation data from Määttä et al., 2020 and shown in Figure 4A

claim: Upregulating the protein expression of genes on chromosomes not affected by aneuploidy serves as a compensatory mechanism to prevent proteotoxicity triggered by the aggregation of non-paired complex members located on the aneuploid chromosome
source: This suggests that upregulating the protein expression of genes on chromosomes not affected by aneuploidy themselves serves as a compensatory mechanism to prevent proteotoxicity triggered by the aggregation of non-paired complex members located on the aneuploid chromosome.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that aggregation-prone proteins show stronger correlations with partners

claim: Aggregation-prone proteins are not related to stronger correlations with their complex partners on other chromosomes when they are encoded on deleted chromosomes
source: Indeed, we observed aggregation-prone proteins to be not related to stronger correlations with their complex partners on other chromosomes when they are encoded on deleted chromosomes (Figure 4A).
evidence: Based on analysis shown in Figure 4A

claim: Deleted aneuploid proteins have significantly stronger correlations with their aggregating co-complex members
source: We found that deleted aneuploid proteins have significantly stronger correlations with their aggregating co-complex members (p=0.045, Wilcoxon test; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Based on Wilcoxon test analysis and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: Promiscuous proteins of amplified chromosomes show weaker correlations with their partners compared to non-promiscuous proteins
source: As expected, we observed weaker correlations for promiscuous proteins of amplified chromosomes (p=6e-16, Wilcoxon test; Figure 4B) further supporting the model in which differential abundance of proteins on other chromosomes is a compensatory mechanism.
evidence: Based on Wilcoxon test analysis and shown in Figure 4B

claim: Proteins co-occurring in many complexes show stronger correlation than proteins found only in a few cases together in the same complex
source: Indeed, we found significant differences in the number of times aneuploid proteins and their positively correlated co-complex members were found together in the same complex vs their uncorrelated or negatively correlated co-complex members (p=2.2e-12 and p=2.8e-14 for chromosomal amplifications, p=0.004 and p=7.4e-05 for deletions; Figure 4C).
evidence: Based on statistical analysis and shown in Figure 4C

claim: Top correlated proteins form complexes that are frequently involved in translation, RNA splicing, RNA processing, and protein complex assembly
source: The analysis revealed that top correlated proteins form complexes that are frequently involved in translation (mainly driven by ribosomal proteins; see Materials and methods section), RNA splicing, RNA processing, and protein complex assembly (Figure 5A; Supplementary file 6).
evidence: Based on functional enrichment analysis and shown in Figure 5A

claim: Top correlations in the deletion cases are related to stronger enrichment scores when compared to their counterparts in the amplification cases
source: We observed that top correlations in the deletion cases are related to stronger enrichment scores when compared to their counterparts in the amplification cases (Figure 5B).
evidence: Based on enrichment score analysis and shown in Figure 5B

claim: Samples with low stoichiometry deviation scores are related to lower survival probabilities in all three tissue types
source: While not significant in every single case we observed a tendency that samples with low stoichiometry deviation scores are related to lower survival probabilities in all three tissue types (Figure 6B) showing that compensation for protein abundance indeed provides a survival advantage to tumors.
evidence: Based on survival analysis and shown in Figure 6B

claim: Ubiquitin-binding proteins and components of the proteasome show significantly higher correlations between their abundances and the stoichiometry deviation scores in two out of three tissues
source: We indeed found that ubiquitin-binding proteins and components of the proteasome show significantly higher correlations between their abundances and the stoichiometry deviation scores in two out of three tissues (Figure 6C; Figure 6—figure supplement 1B), and this tendency still applies when samples are divided into amplification and deletion groups (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Based on correlation analysis and shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B, D

claim: 47–63% and 24–33% of genes on aneuploid chromosomes show expression changes at the transcriptome and proteome level, respectively
source: Here, we conduct an extensive characterization of the transcriptome and proteome in aneuploid human cancers. We show that 47–63% and 24–33% of genes on aneuploid chromosomes show expression changes at the transcriptome and proteome level (Figure 1C), respectively.
evidence: Based on analysis of TCGA/CPTAC data and shown in Figure 1C

claim: 50% and 25% of genes showed copy-number-correlated expression changes at the transcriptome and proteome level in human cancer cells
source: A similar degree of the effect of aneuploidy on expression changes has been previously found in human cancer cells: 50% and 25% of genes showed copy-number-correlated expression changes at the transcriptome and proteome level, respectively (Schukken and Sheltzer, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schukken and Sheltzer, 2021

claim: Up to 70–80% of genes on aneuploid chromosomes changed levels of transcripts and proteins by the degree expected based on chromosome number in yeasts
source: In yeasts, aneuploidy affects a larger fraction of genes. Up to 70–80% of genes on aneuploid chromosomes changed levels of transcripts and proteins by the degree expected based on chromosome number (Dephoure et al., 2014; Gasch et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dephoure et al., 2014 and Gasch et al., 2016

claim: The stronger buffering at the proteome level than transcriptome level is consistently observed independently from the study system
source: However, independently from the study system, the stronger buffering at the proteome level than transcriptome level is consistently observed (Stingele et al., 2012; Dephoure et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Stingele et al., 2012 and Dephoure et al., 2014

claim: In amplification cases, 76.5% and 26.2% of proteomic changes show also differential abundance of the corresponding transcript for aneuploid and other chromosomes, respectively
source: Further, comparison of transcriptome and proteome data reveals that proteomic changes from aneuploid chromosomes could primarily be explained by differential expression of their corresponding genes at the transcriptome level; however, this is not the case for proteomic changes of other, non-aneuploid chromosomes (in amplification cases, 76.5% and 26.2% of proteomic changes, and in deletion cases, 89.9% and 36.2% of the differentially abundant proteins show also differential abundance of the corresponding transcript for aneuploid and other chromosomes, respectively).
evidence: Based on comparison of transcriptomic and proteomic data

claim: In deletion cases, 89.9% and 36.2% of the differentially abundant proteins show also differential abundance of the corresponding transcript for aneuploid and other chromosomes, respectively
source: Further, comparison of transcriptome and proteome data reveals that proteomic changes from aneuploid chromosomes could primarily be explained by differential expression of their corresponding genes at the transcriptome level; however, this is not the case for proteomic changes of other, non-aneuploid chromosomes (in amplification cases, 76.5% and 26.2% of proteomic changes, and in deletion cases, 89.9% and 36.2% of the differentially abundant proteins show also differential abundance of the corresponding transcript for aneuploid and other chromosomes, respectively).
evidence: Based on comparison of transcriptomic and proteomic data

claim: Transcriptional control plays a major role for aneuploid chromosomes while translational or post-translational control has a comparably stronger importance for gene regulation of other chromosomes
source: Together, these observations suggest different levels of control for dosage compensation for aneuploid and other chromosomes. Transcriptional control plays a major role for aneuploid chromosomes while translational or post-translational control has a comparably stronger importance for gene regulation of other chromosomes.
evidence: Inferred from the differential concordance between transcriptomic and proteomic changes

claim: Up to 40% of the differentially abundant proteins physically interact either in a complex or in a binary manner with their partners on the aneuploid chromosome
source: We observe that up to 40% of the typically hundreds and sometimes more than 1000 differentially abundant proteins physically interact either in a complex or in a binary manner with their partners on the aneuploid chromosome.
evidence: Based on analysis of protein complex and PPI data

claim: Targeting essential genes in aneuploid cells eventually results in proliferation defects and activation of cell death pathways
source: It has been shown that targeting essential genes in aneuploid cells eventually results in proliferation defects and activation of cell death pathways (Cohen-Sharir et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cohen-Sharir et al., 2021

claim: Aneuploidy is detrimental for normal cells as it causes stoichiometric imbalances in protein complexes involving proteins encoded on the aneuploid chromosome
source: Typically, aneuploidy is detrimental for normal cells, among other reasons as it causes stoichiometric imbalances in protein complexes involving proteins encoded on the aneuploid chromosome (Brennan et al., 2019; Santaguida and Amon, 2015a).
evidence: Supported by citations to Brennan et al., 2019 and Santaguida and Amon, 2015a

claim: Aneuploidy affects expression of a large number of genes simultaneously by providing additional or diminished copies of genes or decreasing their transcription
source: Aneuploidy, whole-chromosome- or chromosome-arm-level alterations, affects expression of a large number of genes simultaneously - most directly by providing additional or diminished copies of genes in - or decreasing their transcription.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about aneuploidy

claim: Differential DNA methylation and dysregulation of transcription factors mediate aberrant gene expression in cancer
source: Previous studies have revealed the role of epigenetic and transcriptional regulatory mechanisms in cancer. Differential DNA methylation and dysregulation of transcription factors (TFs) mediate aberrant gene expression in cancer (Baylin and Herman, 2000; Ehrlich, 2002; Bushweller, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Baylin and Herman, 2000; Ehrlich, 2002; Bushweller, 2019

claim: Ubiquitination at multiple sites is an efficient signal for degradation
source: Previous studies have suggested that ubiquitination at multiple sites is an efficient signal for degradation (Dimova et al., 2012) and further increase in the number of ubiquitination sites is related to higher binding affinity between protein and proteasome (Lu et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dimova et al., 2012 and Lu et al., 2015

claim: Increase in the number of ubiquitination sites is related to higher binding affinity between protein and proteasome
source: Previous studies have suggested that ubiquitination at multiple sites is an efficient signal for degradation (Dimova et al., 2012) and further increase in the number of ubiquitination sites is related to higher binding affinity between protein and proteasome (Lu et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lu et al., 2015

claim: The main expected detrimental effect of chromosomal amplifications is an excess of protein abundance of complex members leading to an aggregation of the orphan proteins
source: The main expected detrimental effect of chromosomal amplifications is an excess of protein abundance of complex members leading to an aggregation of the orphan proteins (rather than a loss of function of the complex as would be expected for insufficient expression for complex assembly as a consequence of chromosome deletion) (Santaguida et al., 2015b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Santaguida et al., 2015b

claim: Complex organization shapes protein abundance changes in response to CNAs
source: Those observations are in line with previous findings claiming that complex organization shapes protein abundance changes in response to CNAs (Sousa et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sousa et al., 2019

claim: Similar compensatory mechanisms have been previously identified to be induced by focal CNAs
source: Similar compensatory mechanisms have been previously identified to be induced by focal CNAs (Gonçalves et al., 2017; Sousa et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gonçalves et al., 2017 and Sousa et al., 2019

claim: Aneuploidy has an impact on cell proliferation
source: One of the major consequences of aneuploidy is its impact on cell proliferation (Santaguida and Amon, 2015a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Santaguida and Amon, 2015a

claim: 22% of proteins form part of at least one complex in CORUM
source: However, the coverage of proteins with CORUM complex information is rather limited (22% of proteins form part of at least one complex in CORUM).
evidence: Based on analysis of CORUM database coverage

claim: 23% of the translation-related genes are ribosomal genes
source: Among these terms, enrichment of translation is mostly driven by a relatively larger fraction of ribosomal genes among our gene sets (which might not be surprising given that 23% of the translation-related genes are ribosomal genes).
evidence: Based on analysis of gene composition in translation-related functional categories

claim: Protein complex subunits of other chromosomes tend to maintain their abundance levels unless they form a complex with differentially abundant proteins encoded by genes located on the aneuploid chromosome
source: We show that protein complex subunits of other chromosomes tend to maintain their abundance levels unless they form a complex with differentially abundant proteins encoded by genes located on the aneuploid chromosome.
evidence: Based on analysis of protein complex co-abundance patterns

claim: Co-abundance regulation is dependent on aggregation propensity and promiscuity of the aneuploid complex partners
source: We further demonstrate that this co-abundance regulation is dependent on aggregation propensity and promiscuity of the aneuploid complex partners and controlled by post-translational mechanisms.
evidence: Based on analysis of protein features and abundance correlations

claim: Co-abundance regulation is controlled by post-translational mechanisms
source: We further demonstrate that this co-abundance regulation is dependent on aggregation propensity and promiscuity of the aneuploid complex partners and controlled by post-translational mechanisms.
evidence: Based on analysis showing lack of transcriptional/epigenetic control and presence of ubiquitination signals

claim: Coordinated abundance changes of complex partners might prevent aggregation of unpaired complex members
source: Our findings highlight a complementary mechanism acting to deal with the excess amount of expression changes induced by aneuploidy: Coordinated abundance changes of complex partners might prevent aggregation of unpaired complex members.
evidence: Inferred from the observed co-abundance patterns and their relationship to aggregation propensity

claim: Complexes of the cellular core machinery are under functional selection to maintain their stoichiometric balance in aneuploid tumors
source: On the other hand, we observed that complexes of the cellular core machinery are under functional selection to maintain their stoichiometric balance in aneuploid tumors.
evidence: Based on functional enrichment analysis showing specific functions are protected

claim: Compensatory and functional maintenance mechanisms are established through post-translational control
source: Ultimately, we provide evidence that those compensatory and functional maintenance mechanisms are established through post-translational control, and that the degree of success of a tumor to deal with aneuploidy-induced stoichiometric imbalance impacts the activation of cellular protein degradation programs and patient survival.
evidence: Based on ubiquitination analysis and lack of transcriptional/epigenetic signals

claim: The degree of success of a tumor to deal with aneuploidy-induced stoichiometric imbalance impacts the activation of cellular protein degradation programs and patient survival
source: Ultimately, we provide evidence that those compensatory and functional maintenance mechanisms are established through post-translational control, and that the degree of success of a tumor to deal with aneuploidy-induced stoichiometric imbalance impacts the activation of cellular protein degradation programs and patient survival.
evidence: Based on survival analysis and correlation with proteasome/ubiquitin-binding protein abundance
